description: Soy Christopher Bardales, estudiante de Ingeniería de Sistemas y fundador de AIRSTARK. Me apasiona combinar IA, realidad aumentada, 3D y ciencia para crear soluciones innovadoras. Busco personas que quieran construir y experimentar en equipo, especialmente con habilidades en IA/ML, software, ciencia espacial, Unity/3D, diseño, datos o investigación. 🚀 Si te apasiona el espacio y la tecnología, ¡únete a nuestro equipo!
summary:
On a mission to Mars, asking Earth, "Is what I’m feeling serious?" could take 45 minutes for a round-trip exchange. AIRSTARK for Astronauts eliminates that wait.
It is a health-monitoring platform that enables any crew member—regardless of medical training—to understand their physiological state and take action without relying on mission control. The system integrates three layers. First: real-time data from a wearable device (a Galaxy Watch 4, in the demo) is sent to a Supabase database, capturing heart rate and anthropometric indices. Second: a 3D digital twin of the heart—reconstructed from computed tomography (CT) scans—beats in sync with the astronaut’s actual heart rate, transforming abstract figures into something that can be interpreted at a glance. Third: an AI agent, powered by a local language model that operates independently of Earth, explains these metrics in plain language. It also consults a proprietary cardiovascular risk-prediction model, which was trained using data from the Framingham Heart Study and validated by the hospital ethics committee at the Almanzor Hospital in Chiclayo.
While it provides guidance for immediate action, it does not issue medical prescriptions nor does it replace medical personnel; when a clinical decision is required, it escalates the situation with a fully documented clinical picture. The result: medical autonomy in environments where latency makes real-time telemedicine impossible.
details:
NASA's Human Research Program identifies five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile and closed environments. Of these five, the one that defines our solution is distance from Earth, because it is the hazard that turns any other health problem into an emergency.

The reason is latency. In NASA's HERA analog, a crew spent 45 days on a simulated deep space mission with communication delays of up to five minutes each way with Mission Control. On a Mars mission the distance is another order of magnitude. In episode 59 of "Houston We Have a Podcast", emergency physician Erik Antonsen explains that the delay ranges from one to three minutes one way at closest approach to 22 and a half minutes one way at the farthest point: close to 45 minutes between a question and its answer. That is precisely the scenario he describes: delivering appropriate medical care with limited resources and challenging communications.

There is an operational fact on top of this: not every crew flies with a physician aboard. NASA states in the challenge itself that astronauts must be able to self-assess during a mission, and warns that we cannot assume they know how to interpret their own health indicators.

So the real problem is not measurement. The sensors already exist and they are good. The problem is that a number without interpretation is worth nothing 400 million kilometres away from a cardiologist.
AIRSTARK for Astronauts is an autonomous health monitoring and medical assistance platform, designed to work with no connection to Earth. It builds on an architecture our team had already developed to solve an equivalent problem on the ground, in isolated regions with no specialists and no hospital infrastructure, which we have now redirected toward the space environment.

The system works in three chained layers:

LAYER 1 — Real-time data acquisition. A wearable device continuously records the astronaut's vital signs. In our demo we use a Samsung Galaxy Watch 4, which provides heart rate, stress level and anthropometric indices (weight, height, BMI). The data is stored in a PostgreSQL database on Supabase, which acts as the single source of truth for the rest of the system. This layer is sensor-agnostic: any device that exposes its readings can be connected without redesigning anything downstream.

LAYER 2 — Interactive digital twin. From medical imaging (CT scans) we reconstruct a 3D model of the organ. In this version it is the heart, and it beats on screen at the rate the wearable has just measured. This answers directly what the challenge asks for: a visual, animated and interactive tool where health status is understood at a glance rather than read off a table. The twin uses colour coding to show whether values fall within the expected range.

LAYER 3 — Onboard AI agent. A local language model, installed on the crew's own equipment, interprets the data and answers questions in natural language. It is not a generic chatbot: it is connected to models our team trained for specific conditions. In this demo, to a machine learning system for myocardial infarction prevention, built on the Framingham Heart Study and validated by the ethics committee of Red Prestacional Lambayeque and the Cardiology Service of Hospital Nacional Almanzor Aguinaga Asenjo.

The full flow is: the sensor measures, the database records, the digital twin displays, the specialised model evaluates, and the agent explains. The astronaut gets a readable interpretation and, if something falls outside the expected range, supportive guidance on what to do next. All onboard, in seconds, without waiting for Earth.
It is worth being explicit about this, because it shapes the whole design: AIRSTARK does not replace the physician.

The system covers the gap that is empty today. It measures continuously, detects a deviation, explains it in understandable language, and guides the immediate actions any crew member can safely take on their own: stop the activity, control their breathing, repeat the measurement, log the episode, trigger a protocol already approved for the mission, or alert the rest of the crew. That is the stretch where minutes count and where today there is nobody.

What the system deliberately does not do: it does not prescribe medication, does not set dosages, and does not authorise invasive treatments or higher-complexity procedures. Those decisions belong to qualified medical personnel. First, to the physician or medically trained crew member onboard, if the mission has one; failing that, to medical control on Earth.

And this closes the loop with the problem we opened with: escalating to Earth still costs what it costs. At the farthest point of Mars' orbit that is 22 and a half minutes for the query to arrive and as long again for the answer to come back. So the system does not try to replace that consultation, it tries to make it count. When the astronaut escalates, they are not sending a question: they are sending a documented case, with the historical series of vital signs, the clinical model's assessment and a description of the episode. The physician on Earth answers once, with complete information, instead of spending two or three 45-minute cycles asking the basics.

Put briefly: the system handles what is immediate and reversible; medical personnel decide what is clinical and irreversible. And when that second decision has to come from Earth, AIRSTARK reduces the number of latency cycles needed to reach it.
Our differentiator is not the wearable or the visualisation. It is the onboard intelligence architecture: a local language model acting as interpreter and orchestrator, connected to a set of specialised clinical models trained by our own team.

The distinction matters. A general language model can sound convincing about health without any clinical grounding. A specialised clinical model is rigorous but cannot explain itself to a non-specialist. We separate the two functions: the specialised model evaluates, the language model translates. And because both run onboard, latency with Earth stops being a factor.

This also makes the system extensible by design. We start with the heart because that is where we have a trained and validated model. Next comes a neurological one, a respiratory one, one for bone density. Each new model joins as another module the agent can query, with no need to rebuild the platform. We are not building a tool for one disease: we are building the place where those tools coexist and become understandable.

The second creative element is the digital twin as a language. Seeing your own heart beating at the rhythm you have just measured communicates your health state in a way no number achieves. It is the difference between reading "102 bpm" and watching the organ race.
For the crew, the benefit is autonomy: immediate self-assessment, without depending on a link that may take 45 minutes to complete one cycle or on having a physician among the crew. It shortens the gap between a warning sign appearing and someone interpreting it, which is exactly where the margin for action is lost in an emergency.

For mission control on Earth, the benefit is continuity: a structured historical record of each crew member's evolution, available for review whenever communication allows. Asynchrony stops meaning lost information.

For long-mission design, the impact is structural. If a crew can resolve part of its medical decisions onboard, the risk profile of deep space missions changes. This is one of the conditions that must be solved for Mars to be viable.

And there is an impact back on Earth that we do not consider secondary. This architecture was born solving the same problem in isolated communities with no specialists and no high-cost hospital infrastructure. The technology we build for an astronaut 400 million kilometres away is the same technology that serves a patient in a rural community six hours from the nearest hospital. The cardiovascular model used in this demo was trained and validated in precisely that context, in a public hospital in northern Peru.
Latency and autonomy. This was our starting constraint, not an afterthought. It is why we ruled out any architecture depending on a cloud API: if the system needs a link to Earth in order to answer, it does not solve the scenario we care about.

Onboard compute limits. A local model has to run on the hardware available in a spacecraft, not in a data centre. This constrains model size and forces us to optimise rather than assume unlimited resources.

Clinical scope and responsibility. This was a design decision from day one, not a disclaimer bolted on at the end, and it is set out in the "Scope of the system" section above. The fact that our cardiovascular model holds hospital ethics committee validation is part of that same stance: we prefer a narrower, defensible scope over a broad one with nothing behind it.

False positives. In a confined environment a wrong alert has a real cost: it creates anxiety and erodes trust in the system. We prefer a system that explains with nuance over one that alarms with confidence.

Users without medical training. The challenge asks for this explicitly and we put it at the centre of the design: plain language, colour coding, anatomical visualisation rather than data tables.

Extensibility. Every architectural decision was made assuming ten clinical models tomorrow instead of one. That is why the agent queries models as independent modules.

Cost. We kept the low-cost methodology the platform was born with. We use consumer hardware and open technologies so the solution stays replicable and does not depend on specialised equipment.
The current version demonstrates the full cycle on one organ. The next stages are: adding further clinical models (neurological, respiratory, bone density) to the set the agent can query; expanding the digital twin library to cover those systems; integrating medical-grade sensors alongside the consumer wearable; and validating the whole in an isolation analog environment, which is the path NASA itself uses to test technology before flying it.
